newsitem.title: USA: House prober wants papers on Quayle fundraiser.
newsitem.headline: House prober wants papers on Quayle fundraiser.

text.p: A Democratic congressman investigating campaign fund abuses called on Monday for an inquiry into a reception held for Republican campaign donors at former Vice President Dan Quayle's official residence.

Representative Henry Waxman of California, who is senior minority member of the House committee looking into improper funds made to Democrats, said he wanted the committee also to investigate fund raising at the vice presidential home.
He released a letter to Representative Dan Burton, the Indiana Republican who heads the House Government Reform and Oversight committee they serve on, to join him in the probe.
Waxman made public documents that indicated a reception was held on the lawn of the vice presidential mansion Sept. 23, 1990 for the Republican Senatorial Inner Circle.
The Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee which sponors the Inner Circle group that costs $1,000 to join said the Quayle reception was "legal and ethical."

"The Democrats have been caught with both hands and both arms in this illegal fund-raising cookie jar," said committee spokesman Mike Russell, who added that they are trying to criticise "legal and ethical fund-raising events" involving Republicans.
Waxman noted that Burton had said on ABC's "This Week" programme Sunday there was a question of legality if government facilities at the White House were used to solicit campaign donations.
Burton was referring to a controversy over President Bill Clinton's role in allowing contributors to stay in the Lincoln Bedroom, golf with him or join in coffee chats at the White House.
Clinton has denied the Lincoln Bedroom was for sale or that funds were solicited from the White House. It is illegal to use government facilities to seek partisan political funds.

Waxman said the invitation to Republican Inner Circle members written by Sen. Don Nickles, an Oklahoma Republican, "falls squarely within the scope of the committee's investigation into improper fund-raising activities." Nickles is a former chairman of the Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee.
"Indeed, they appear to be the most explicit evidence of the use of federal property for fund raising that has yet come to light," Waxman said of the invitation to Republican donors.
There was no comment immediately available from the Republican Senatorial Campaign Committee which sponors the Inner Circle group which said that it costs $1,000 to join the organisation.
